3	Joshua Meyers 
4	+1 617 310 0767
5	joshua.meyers@jpmorgan.com 
6	I spent the week marketing across Europe with the inimitable Scott Silver. Sentiment around the AI Hardware/Semis trade remains frustrated, with most investors interested to buy/positively inclined (doubly so after bullish takes from Communicopia, Citi, and JPM conferences), but few materially upweighting/re-grossing. Key reasons folks remain sidelined are: 1) Frontier model worries (How serious a danger is misalignment, really? Will IPOs happen/will there ultimately be money to fund C28 capex? Will value really continue to flow to frontier operators? Is Jev a risk?); 2) Macro, Politics and War (Inflation, Rates, Oil, bipartisan AI hate, Iran, Yemen, Ukraine); and 3) Quite a few are still sitting on gains they want to protect. We spent as much time talking about these sorts of issues as we did stocks, and similar to what I mentioned in our Zoom Out call last week, folks aren’t leaving chats with any clearer action points. 
7	Some broad themes, though: 
8	· Catalysts are being closely watched: MU results (feedback so far is that even a good print may be faded); Further domestic developments on alignment; A long-awaited S-1; A possible FCC transceiver ban (big for the optical names, if it happens); Investor days & OCP (SNPS 9/30 Analyst Day, HPE 9/30 Networking Day, MRVL 10/6 Investor Day, AMAT 10/13 Investor Day, CLS 10/27 Analyst Day, etc); Earnings (if this is another “beat and raise and stocks go down” quarter, it could be a painful year-end); New restrictions/pauses on data center builds; Custom silicon ramps (Trainium 3, Maia 3, Mediatek TPUv6t, etc.); and continued success of the Muse rollout (Continued success or do they run into problems? And will competition emerge?). 
9	· Bit by bit Investors are starting to use more agents, and they’re impressed to the point where some are even saying they will try foregoing a junior hire in favor of becoming more reliant on those agents. Investors are also more excited about consumer agentic use cases - particularly the success of Muse. Regardless of whether META ends up being the winner (many expect frontier labs to offer fast-follower consumer agents soon), it’s among the first real proof of concept that there’s strong consumer interest in the product. 
10	· Memory still seems broadly liked, though not everyone is interested to re-gross– especially with MU back over $1000. The key question we hear is how the stock can work if price growth is flattening, and with growing uncertainty around demand (de-specing worries, concerns that HBM 12-Hi and 16-Hi may not be popular, confusion around R&D focused on lowering HBM and broader memory intensity). There is also pushback that it’s too early for LTAs to allow a re-rating a la the HDD industry, and many folks complain that WFE and HDD names can’t work well until DRAM sentiment improves conclusively. 
11	· CPU & GPU. CPU is quite in-favor at the moment because “agents need computers” and “Muse is giving you another computer for free.” Preference seems to be for AMD > INTC > others; a few brave souls are short ARM, but there’s no consensus there – or on QCOM, either. Quite a few investors, however, asked how much longer the trade can last … guess it depends where you are on peak AMD earnings power… “What gets NVDA working?” and “What gets AVGO working?” were also among the most common questions we got. There’s no consensus from conversations, but I will say that sentiment around NVDA seems better, and that for AVGO many US investors are more concerned about CSP capex than about Mediatek. 
12	· Networking. No clear consensus. We haven’t had many conversations were folks sounded very interested in laggards like CRDO and CLS, and several folks expressed surprise at ANET’s resilience. There is more interest in LITE/COHR (perhaps because of their ECOC commentary and roadshowing) as NPO picks and shovels plays, though only a few aggressive investors told us they’ve gotten more long. Nokia also seems to have a strong following, though quite a few investors pushed back on a view that Nokia can materially outperform CIEN (given the latter is a favorite of US investors, and has always commanded a deserve multiple premium)…my sense is that a lot of US hedge funds are long Nokia. 
13	· MRVL & QCOM kept coming up as longs, and there seems to be a lot of interest in EDA (especially CDNS), particularly given some recent SaaS stock outperformance. As usual (it’s Europe), Analog came up in nearly every conversation, but folks didn’t sound convicted on the sector. 
14	I also wanted again to share redacted results to my MU Buyside Survey. Folks who participated only expect the team to announce ~35% of bits under LTA (but with upside to something closer to 50% by year-end). In conversations so far, folks don’t seem to view higher LTA coverage or discussion of capital return as material upside catalysts, which I find surprising… 
15	Positioning: Hot or Not… 
16	JPM positioning Intel concedes that rising rates have capped upside, but they haven’t dented the progress we’ve seen in the AI trade. That said, there was little change in positioning WoW, with net positioning remaining somewhat light, and performance middling (outside of Quants doing well). Asia selling picked up, but North America net flows were flat on the week, and our Trade Positioning Monitor picked up a bit. Rate-sensitives are naturally seeing persistent selling (Real Estate, Telecom, and Utilities among the most net sold industries over the past 20d, with Utes/Telecom positioning at historical lows). Health Care crowding performance took another leg lower (L-S return spread -7% past 5d; -6% MTD), and Biotech selling reflects positioning skews (reach out for the full details). Financials are seeing some buy-the-dip (in LC banks, not regionals). Tech, meanwhile, continues to see Mag 7 re-risking and semis buying, with retail sentiment turning back up: Tech enthusiasm improved meaningfully alongside the price bounce; TMT drove much of the net buying, with Mag7 bought nearly ~3z over the past 5d (and 20d), Semis +2z, and Software +1z. Retail sentiment for Semis vs. Software has rebounded MTD after hitting >12m lows in early Sep, and while it’s only back to around average levels, it leaves room for further upside if AI optimism persists. 
17	Within semis, positioning remains crowded in INTC and TSMC. MU is still a crowded long, but has been seeing log selling; LRCX is also a crowded long, but conversely has been seeing some new buying/covering. NVDA, AMD and AMAT are also rather crowded longs. AVGO seems increasingly to be a source of funding. MCHP and KLAC have again seen shorts pick up. In Hardware, long crowding in HDDs seems actually to have picked up, though APH long crowding has come of a bit. FLEX & JBL are also quite crowded longs, while shorts have picked up materially in DELL. 
18	Watchpoints (let me know what I’m missing!) 
19	· Joseph Cardoso hosts a call tomorrow at 11am ET to share ECOC takeaways. Register here. 
20	· One of the Frontier LLM companies hosts its Developer Day on Tuesday. Some investors expect them to announce a new personal AI agent to compete with META Muse. 
21	· On Wednesday Sept 30 we also have SNPS’ Analyst Day and HPE’s Networking Event, in addition to JBL earnings bmo and MU earnings amc. 
22	· Gokul Hariharan is in the US to talk Asia Tech with investors the week of October 5. Reach out to your generalist sales if you want to meet 1x1 or join a lunch of drinks event. 
23	· On Tuesday, Oct 6, MRVL hosts its Investor Day. 
24	· On Friday, Oct 9 Gokul Hariharan and Joe Cardoso host a US/Asia Hardware & Networking Equipment Group Lunch at 12:30pm. Request a seat here. 
25	· On October 13, Joseph Cardoso hosts group meetings at OCP with CRDO, JBL, KEYS, TEL & 650 Group. Request a spot here. AMAT will also hold its Investor Day on that date. 
26	· We’re hosting an Asia Robotics & Automation Tour in Korea & China Oct 12~14. More details here. 
27	· Thu Oct 15 SMTC hosts its Analyst Day/Data Center Teach-in. 
28	· CLS hosts its Analyst Day on October 27. 
29	· We’ll host our annual Global Tech Conf in Asia Nov 16~18 in Hong Kong, with nearly 200 companies across A&D, Auto/EV, Consumer/Media, Healthcare, Robotics, Internet and Hard Tech. You can find more details here. I’ll be at the event, and marketing in Asia, so let me know if you want to meet up! 
30	Key Research from the week… 
31	Joe Cardoso’s takeaways from ECOC meetings with CIEN, COHR, CRDO, CSCO & LITE. Here 
32	CIEN (Brodie Gage, EVP, Chief Product and Technology Officer): As power and datacenter locations increasingly dictate deployment plans, hyperscalers see scale-across distances widening – raising both ASPs and TAM. The team also expects more hyperscaler wins shortly; and service providers are also assessing the product. Continued vertical integration is helping to support cost and performance advantages. The team’s 2027 revenue outlook is explicitly framed as a supply floor, with pump lasers (980nm for EDFAs, 1440nm for Raman) the most acute bottleneck, while ASIC supply is not a constraint. NPO and intra-data center represent upside to the long-term outlook, with less than $500mn of combined revenue currently embedded in 2029 guidance. 
33	COHR (Jim Anderson, CEO; Dr. Sanjai Parthasarathi, CMO; Dr. Christopher Dorman, EVP, Industrial): The team unveiled PhotonLink, an integrated optics platform spanning CPO, NPO, and chip-to-chip connectivity, which management sizes at $30bn of SAM by end of decade, supporting a total COHR SAM of $90bn. Engagement intensity has ramped significantly over the last 6-12 months, with 10+ unique CPO customers, 10+ NPO customers, and 5+ chip-to-chip engagements — scale-out CPO begins ramping in the Dec-26 quarter, scale-up CPO and NPO follow in 2HC27, and chip-to-chip materializes toward 2029-30. On pump lasers, packaging remains the key bottleneck, with COHR and one other supplier the only material players, and COHR is leveraging the supply-demand imbalance to push higher-margin integrated multi-rail solutions. Content opportunity is compelling — up to ~$15k per 100T chip for a full PhotonLink CPO/NPO solution using 200G per optical lane. 
34	CRDO (CFO Dan Fleming) pushed back on AEC growth concerns, attributing the guided mid-single-digit sequential growth in fiscal 2H27 to project timing and the 800G-to-1.6T transition, with 1.6T becoming a more meaningful driver in FY28. Optics is the bigger story - management sees it potentially reaching 30-50% of revenue next fiscal year, underpinned by a significant cost advantage (optical DSP/PIC cost of ~＄20 vs. ~＄100 for a standard 800G TRx) and a telemetry premium that drives ZF optics gross margins to ~68% vs. ~40% for best-in-class TRx peers. The OmniConnect/Positron opportunity is flagged as a large underappreciated catalyst — if Positron ships hundreds of thousands of systems, it could become a 10%+ customer in FY28 at ~$2k of content per system. Manufacturing footprint, laser supply, and related supply secured over the last 9-12 months positions CRDO to capture ~10% market share in a TAM heading toward 175mn optical module units by end of decade. 
35	CSCO (Tom Williams, VP, Product Management, Acacia) & Lorenzo Ghioni (VP, Product Management, Optical Systems): The 800G ZR/ZR+ portfolio continues to gain share (75k+ modules shipped, tracking above 400G share levels), with the next growth leg coming from 400G-to-800G upgrades; 1.6T scale is a mid-2028 story as the broader ecosystem catches up. Multi-rail qualifications are targeted for year-end with hyperscaler deployments beginning early 2027, while integrated optical solutions are becoming a strategic differentiator as hyperscalers consolidate their vendor base. On CPO/NPO, CSCO is investing in both but has no firm view yet on where volumes become meaningful, with the ultimate gating factor being the right combination of performance, reliability, and manufacturability at scale. Supply constraints remain manageable via long-term agreements and supplier diversification, with pump-laser bottlenecks driven by finishing/packaging capacity rather than the chip itself. 
36	LITE (CEO Michael Hurlston): The team remains highly bullish on NPO, framing it as entirely incremental to its $40 EPS framework, with five active engagements (two high-power ELS at ~400mW, three medium-power ILS at ~150-200mW) and pricing on newer programs running 1.3-1.4x higher than the initial Nvidia program. The key near-term constraint is capacity — LITE can currently supply only ~30% of the laser demand it sees for 2027, with Caswell expansion underway ahead of a new facility coming online in 2028. The Google OCS opportunity is expected to double in 2027 vs. 2026, with the merchant-addressable portion expanding 1.5-2.0x, and LITE is sole-sourced on a higher port-count inference SKU with shipments expected around mid-CY27 and a meaningful FY28 contribution. VCSELs are seen as better suited for scale-in (motherboard-level XPU/HBM disaggregation) rather than scale-up applications. 
37	ADI: Harlan Takeaways From All Stars Conference — Confident DD% Growth Into FY27 With Broadening Recovery. Here 
38	Harlan Sur hosted ADI CFO Richard Puccio at our U.S. All Stars Conference in London on Tuesday. Management reiterated confidence in double-digit FY27 growth (Street at +22%YoY) underpinned by accelerating design-win momentum (FY26 design wins tracking above FY25's +20% growth) and Maxim synergies on track to exceed the original $1b target by 2027 (~$700M exiting FY26). The cyclical recovery has broadened meaningfully across all end-markets and geographies, with management now guiding to an above-seasonal 1Q27 (vs. typical MSD% QoQ decline) - a notable positive signal. On the data center side, ADI's business is tracking at a ~$2b annualized run-rate, with stage-two power delivery (grid-to-chip) emerging as the key long-term growth driver alongside durable optical (400G/800G à 1.6T à 3.2T), while A&D has nearly doubled to a ~$2B run-rate in just a year, and management sees double-digit growth sustainable for the next decade. Channel inventory remains below ADI's 6-7 week target despite intentional builds (sell-through accelerating faster than expected), and with 50%+ of industrial subsegments still double-digits below historical consumption, replenishment upside remains largely in front of the stock. Importantly, Puccio emphasized that ADI’s pricing actions this year have been intended to counteract sustained input-cost inflation rather than to expand margins. 
39	ARM: Harlan's All Stars Takeaways — AGI CPU Ramp and DC Royalty Momentum Accelerating. Here 
40	Harlan Sur hosted ARM IR Ian Thornton at our U.S. All Stars Conference in London yesterday. The key headline is increased confidence (vs. the last earnings call) in securing additional 3nm AGI CPU supply to drive >$1b in committed chip sales in FY27-FY28, with total demand still tracking >$2b (META is the primary customer). The initial AGI CPU ramp is on track for $100m+ in F4Q27 (March quarter), with the next-gen 2nm AGI CPU progressing well and targeting initial deployment in 2H CY27; the one watch item is that securing additional supply could pressure GMs modestly below the high-30% target as wafer/substrate/packaging costs rise, though the team is explicitly prioritizing share gains over near-term margins. On the royalty side, cloud/AI royalties are growing 2x YoY and ARM server CPU royalties are on track to exceed 10% of total royalties in FY27, with further tailwinds from SmartNIC/DPU, networking, and storage programs as next-gen GPU/XPU deployments accelerate in 2H. Longer-term, the embedded segment adds another growth layer via Ethos NPU penetration in MCU/MPU families targeting physical AI, robotics, and edge ML applications (+15-20% royalty tailwind). 
41	P: Joe Raises TP on Strong Analyst Day Takeaways. Here 
42	Joseph Cardoso was pleased with what heard from P's Financial Analyst Meeting in Santa Clara past week, where management laid out a preliminary FY28 revenue guide of $7~7.3bn (+39-45%YoY - well ahead of consensus at $6.2bn) with operating margins of 24-26% (v. consensus 21.3%); these together imply 80-100%YoY OI growth. The growth story is now framed around four vectors: Core & Core AI (enterprise storage share gains + AI-driven demand), Modern Data Software (data governance/AI readiness), Scale AI (FlashBlade//EXA for neoclouds and frontier model builders where storage is the GPU bottleneck), and Hyperscale Solutions (DirectFlash under hyperscaler storage stacks, with HDD replacement optionality as NAND pricing normalizes). TAM is expected to nearly double from $108b this year to $207b by 2030 (high-teens CAGR), with new growth vectors targeted to reach ~20% of total revenue by FY30 and subscription ARR growing at a >20% 3-year CAGR. Joe bumps his forecast FY28E EPS +24% to $4.35 and sees the Rule of 40 score sustaining at 50-70 through FY30, supporting the ~29x P/E multiple on FY28E EPS underpinning his new price target. 
43	TXN: Harlan's All Stars Takeaways — Broad Demand Recovery With DC Doubling. Here 
44	Harlan Sur hosted TXN IR head Mike Beckman at our U.S. All Stars Conference in London yesterday. The key message was broad-based demand strength across industrial, auto, DC, and consumer, with similar strong YoY growth trajectories guided for Q3 following a strong Q2. The data center business is the standout, tracking at a ~$3b annualized run-rate and on track potentially to double this year, driven by TXN's full power-tree portfolio (GaN, BCD, SiGe, CMOS) spanning grid-to-processor, plus a broad catalog of timing, data conversion, and amplifier products populating compute/networking boards. On pricing, TXN has put in place analog price increases effective end of Q4, with broader analog/power/MCU hikes being negotiated for next year — a forward GM tailwind as customers scramble to lock in supply assurance amid an increasingly constrained competitor landscape. Critically, while peers face supply constraints, TXN has ~$25b in revenue capacity today with RFAB2, Sherman 1, and Lehi 1 running, and the potential to double that as Sherman 2 and Lehi 2 come online — a structural share-gain setup that underpins the OW thesis. 
45	And in Asia Jay Kwon is out with a 9-point memory Bull/Bear, and introducing a DCM framework for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix that still shows an extreme equity upside symmetry (extreme bull is 110~200% upside; extreme bear is -5~20%; his base case is 60~130% upside over 18 months). He probes AI capex sustainability (and implied exposure of AI to memory), HBM de-spec (not thesis-breaking), NAND use cases, criticality of LTAs, Capex and more. Worth your time! Separately he updates his HBM model in this note. 
46	Key News & Reads from the week... 
47	The Surprising Reasons China Is Skeptical of A.I. Safety Calls. For most of China, American doomsday warnings feel remote, foreign, and suspiciously convenient — the Communist Party's confidence in its physical control over technology makes the idea of uncontrollable AI nearly incomprehensible, while calls to restrict China's chip access make safety warnings look like "fear marketing" meant to protect the U.S. lead. Yet Beijing is quietly tightening the screws anyway, with new rogue-agent guidelines, a draft cybercrime law, and an updated AI Safety Governance Framework that echoes Silicon Valley's fears about recursive self-improvement - The New York Times 
48	How to Know When the AI Boom Is About to Go Bust. The AI boom's real risk isn't power shortages or rogue agents—it's that booms only survive as long as fresh capital keeps flowing, and history from dot-com burn rates to Freddie Mac's 2007 equity scramble shows busts start the moment that window closes. Watch for "funding gap" to re-enter the vernacular: that's the tell that the capital markets have stopped believing the story before the technologists do – The Wall Street Journal 
49	Goldman: hyperscaler AI capex to jump 50% to $1.2T in 2027. Goldman Sachs strategists forecast AI infrastructure spending by the five largest US hyperscalers will reach $1.2T in 2027 — 'a larger share of GDP than any technological investment cycle since the railroad build-out.' JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon separately said hyperscalers could spend $1T next year, up from $700B in 2026 - Bloomberg 
50	AI build-out on track to become the biggest economic bet in US history. Brookings estimates put total data-center and AI infrastructure investment at $10.3T from 2025–2032 — ~3.6% of GDP per year, dwarfing railroads, highways, and the 1990s fiber build. FactSet estimates the five big hyperscalers will spend $4.2T through 2029, increasingly debt-financed through thin-disclosure off-balance-sheet vehicles - The Wall Street Journal 
51	Debt-hungry AI companies face increased risk as bond yields spike. With Treasury yields climbing to their highest since 2007, the AI infrastructure buildout is about to get even more expensive. JPMorgan Chase estimated in June that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued through 2030, as data center companies and others tied to the AI boom race to build up capacity. So far companies have been willing to absorb the higher debt costs, but some investors say they’re starting to worry about future financings - CNBC 
52	Nvidia's Rubin volume ramp slips to 2027 on HBM4 yield bottleneck. Low HBM4 yields remain the binding constraint on Nvidia's next-generation Rubin platform, pushing volume ramp into 2027 and keeping Blackwell dominant through 2026. Suppliers may shift Rubin from 12-high to 8-high HBM4 stacks to ease yield pressure - TrendForce 
53	ByteDance gained access to 2,304 Nvidia B200 chips through Nscale's Norway data center. Nscale disclosed — via a $105M Macquarie loan document, not its $35B IPO S-1 — that ByteDance's Singaporean subsidiary contributed 73% of its 2025 revenue and held access to 2,304 B200 GPUs at its Glomfjord, Norway facility. The arrangement appears legal because ByteDance rented overseas compute rather than importing restricted chips — a major cloud-compute loophole in export controls - Tom's Hardware 
54	Huawei's Kirin 9050 Pro narrows Apple's chip lead to three years without EUV, Bernstein finds. Bernstein estimated Huawei's newest processor — judged to be made on older SMIC DUV manufacturing — beat Apple's 2023 A17 Pro on multicore and trails the current A20 Pro by ~30%, shrinking the gap from four years to three via stacked-logic and architectural techniques rather than transistor shrinks - Seoul Economic Daily 
55	Xiaomi debuts open-weight omnimodal models MiMo-V2.6 Pro and Flash; Pro allegedly performs “on par with Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol across most agent benchmarks.” Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6 series is a newly released, fully open-sourced family of natively omnimodal AI models — including MiMo-V2.6-Pro, MiMo-V2.6-Flash, and an UltraSpeed variant delivering up to 20x faster output — trained using scaled reinforcement learning across coding, visual, agentic, and cyber tasks. MiMo-V2.6-Pro now ranks as the highest-scoring open-source model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (46.32), competing closely with frontier closed models like Claude Opus 5 and GPT 6 Astra, while maintaining the same API pricing as its predecessor. Beyond software engineering, the models demonstrate broad multimodal capabilities spanning 3D world-building, robotics simulation, frontend design, video production, music composition, and scientific research — positioning Xiaomi as a serious open-source challenger in the frontier AI race - Xiaomi 
56	Alibaba Unveils AI Chip to Drive Global Data Center Buildout. Alibaba is committed to spending more than $53 billion over a three-year period to expand its AI capabilities and has set a target of 20 gigawatts of data center capacity for its Alibaba Cloud service globally by 2032. The company today outlined a new Zhenwu V900 accelerator that it says triples the performance of its predecessor. From Alibaba’s T-Head division, it can be combined in clusters of up to 500,000 units to power frontier-model training – Reuters 
57	Gartner predicts 55 percent of enterprise VMware users will be investigating an exit by 2029 (up from 25% now) – The Register 
58	Intel CEO: AI-driven CPU demand lets Intel serve only ~50% of customer orders. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan told Splunk's .conf26 that CPU demand is so strong Intel can supply only about half of what customers ask for, attributing the shortfall to AI inference and agentic workloads rather than GPU training - Ctech 
59	SemiAnalysis: The Chinese AI Infrastructure Boom — Introducing the China Datacenter Model. SemiAnalysis launched a full datacenter capacity model for China, tracking domestic GPU/ASIC builds, power constraints, and the scale of the non-Nvidia AI infrastructure rollout — the week's biggest China-infrastructure analysis piece - SemiAnalysis 
60	Tiered Model Pricing Is Broadening AI Adoption; Limited Impact by Jev. Frontier labs and Deepseek all cut API prices in September, driven by genuine efficiency gains - faster token generation, cheaper cached inputs, smaller KV caches, and sparser MoE activation - rather than margin compression at the frontier. Independent benchmarking (Artificial Analysis) confirms real cost-per-task reductions (e.g., Sol's cost fell from $1.99 to $1.06) at unchanged capability, while frontier-tier pricing (Opus 5.5 max, Astra, Fable 5.1 at $10/$50) has held steady, indicating tiered segmentation rather than industry-wide deflation. This dynamic is expanding the addressable market: previously cost-prohibitive applications and consumer agent use cases (via cheap high-volume model tiers like Jev at $0.0004/call) are now viable, letting developers mix flagship and low-cost models across workflow steps. Continued hardware (TPU v8, Vera Rubin) and software-level efficiency gains - potentially compounded by AI-assisted model development (RSI) - should sustain falling unit inference costs alongside growing usage and compute demand, supporting a volume-driven rather than pricing-power-driven growth thesis for AI infrastructure. Most Jev activity is still experimental. - FundaAI
